```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5,
                      eval = requireNamespace("treeshapesim", quietly = TRUE))
```

Methods that estimate a rate of trait evolution for each branch of a tree are increasingly
used to ask where and why evolution sped up or slowed down. Whether they can answer such
questions depends on how well they recover rates that are known, and that requires data
simulated with known rates. This vignette shows the three ways comdynamite generates rates
that vary among branches, and how well two estimators recover them:

1. rates as a statistical model of their own, with `trait_rates()`;
2. rates that follow the history of a discrete character along the tree, such as habitat or
   region, with `trait_mk()` and `history_rates()`;
3. rates that follow ecological dynamics, the turnover of partners in a simulated
   metacommunity (`turnover_rates()`) or the trophic level in a food web
   (`food_web_rates()`).

All of them give one rate per branch, which `trait_rates(edge_rates = )` turns into trait
values at the tips and nodes. The estimates in the last part were computed in advance with
[`data-raw/vignette_rates.R`](https://github.com/diogoprov/comdynamite/blob/main/data-raw/vignette_rates.R),
which needs RRphylo and mvMORPH; the rest runs here.

```{r setup}
library(comdynamite)
set.seed(7)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(40)

# colour of each branch by the logarithm of its rate, from slow (dark) to fast (light)
plot_rates <- function(tree, rates, main = "") {
  pal <- grDevices::hcl.colors(30, "viridis")
  col <- if (diff(range(rates)) > 0) pal[cut(log(rates), 30, labels = FALSE)] else pal[15]
  ape::plot.phylo(tree, edge.color = col, edge.width = 2.5, show.tip.label = FALSE,
                  main = main)
}
```

## Rates as a model

`trait_rates()` draws the rate of each branch from one of three models: discrete shifts that
multiply the rate and pass to the descendants (`"shift"`), a rate that drifts as geometric
Brownian motion along the tree (`"gbm"`), or rates drawn independently for each branch
(`"iid"`). The trait then evolves by Brownian motion with that rate on each branch.

```{r models, fig.height = 3.5}
shift <- trait_rates(tree, "shift", shifts = 2, shift_size = c(8, 1 / 8))
gbm <- trait_rates(tree, "gbm", rate_sd = 0.8)
iid <- trait_rates(tree, "iid", rate_sd = 0.8)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
plot_rates(tree, shift$edge_rate, "shift")
plot_rates(tree, gbm$edge_rate, "gbm")
plot_rates(tree, iid$edge_rate, "iid")
par(op)
```

Each result keeps the rates (`edge_rate`), the trait values at the tips (`tips`) and nodes
(`nodes`), and the shifts, so the truth is available for any comparison.

## Rates from a history along the tree

Ecological hypotheses about rates are often about the history of lineages: evolution faster
in one habitat than another, a burst after colonising a new region, or a slowdown as
lineages accumulate in the same region. `trait_mk()` simulates the history of a discrete
character along the tree, and `history_rates()` turns it into the rate of each branch, the
mean over the branch of a rate that depends on the history at each moment.

```{r history}
habitat <- trait_mk(tree, q = 0.5, states = c("forest", "open"))
state <- history_rates(habitat, "state", state_rates = c(forest = 1, open = 5))
burst <- history_rates(habitat, "burst", burst = 9, decay = 0.1)
sympatry <- history_rates(habitat, "sympatry", r = -0.1)
summary(cbind(state, burst, sympatry))
```

With `"state"`, each habitat has its own rate, as in Brownian motion with several regimes
(O'Meara et al. 2006). With `"burst"`, each change of habitat multiplies the rate, and the
excess decays with time, along the descending branches too, following the expectation that
selection is strongest when a lineage first adapts to a new community (McPeek 2017). With
`"sympatry"`, the rate falls as more lineages share the same state, the diversity-dependent
model with biogeography of Drury et al. (2016); `data-raw/validation_sympatry.R` checks it
against RPANDA.

```{r history-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
plot_rates(tree, state, "state")
plot_rates(tree, burst, "burst")
plot_rates(tree, sympatry, "sympatry")
par(op)
x <- trait_rates(habitat, edge_rates = state)
head(x$tips)
```

## Rates from ecological dynamics

The metacommunity of `simulate_metacommunity()` runs in ecological time among the species at
the tips, so it cannot inform internal branches. `turnover_rates()` uses it for the tip
branches: `partner_turnover()` counts how often other species enter or leave the sites where
each species lives, and over the last `window` units of time of each tip branch the rate is
`sigma2 * (1 + k * turnover)`. How much branch time the ecological dynamics represent is a
choice, set by `window`; by default it is the whole tip branch.

```{r turnover}
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(20), species_traits(tree),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 400,
                              record_steps = seq(200, 400, 10), extirpation = 0.02)
rates <- turnover_rates(sim, k = 100)
summary(attr(rates, "turnover"))
x <- trait_rates(tree, edge_rates = rates)
```

`food_web_rates()` does the same with the food web of `food_web_dynamics()`: each tip belongs
to a trophic level, and its tip branch evolves faster the faster the mean trait of its level
changed. These speeds are directional changes under selection, not Brownian variances, so
they set relative rates among levels, scaled by `k`.

```{r food-web}
web <- food_web_dynamics(seq(0, 4000, by = 20), init = c(R = 50, N = 0.1, P = 0.1),
                         traits = c(R = 10, N = 4, P = 6), introductions = c(P = 2000),
                         dt = 0.5)
levels <- sample(c("R", "N", "P"), ape::Ntip(tree), replace = TRUE)
rates <- food_web_rates(web, tree, levels, k = 500)
attr(rates, "speed")
```

## Recovering the rates

```{r results}
res <- readRDS("branch-rates.rds")
```

**RRphylo under the three models.** RRphylo (Castiglione et al. 2018) estimates a rate per
branch by phylogenetic ridge regression. Over 30 trees of 60 species per model, the mean
Spearman correlations were:

```{r results-models}
aggregate(cbind(with_change, estimated, ceiling) ~ model, res$models,
          function(v) round(mean(v), 2))
```

`with_change` is the correlation between the rate RRphylo estimates and the change that
actually happened on each branch, per unit length; `estimated`, between its absolute value
and the true rate; and `ceiling`, between the true rate and the realised change, scaled by
the square root of the branch length. The ceiling is the most any method can achieve from
one realisation of the process per branch, since a fast branch can still change little by
chance, and it is low. RRphylo follows the change that happened, but its rates say little
about the rate that generated it.

**Regimes.** When the history is known, the rate of each state can be estimated by Brownian
motion with several regimes (O'Meara et al. 2006), here with `mvMORPH::mvBM(model = "BMM")`
(Clavel et al. 2015) on the true history, over 30 trees of 60 species per true ratio:

```{r results-regimes, fig.height = 4}
aggregate(estimated ~ ratio, res$regimes, function(v) round(stats::median(v), 2))
boxplot(estimated ~ ratio, res$regimes, log = "y", xlab = "True ratio (open / forest)",
        ylab = "Estimated ratio", col = "grey90")
points(1:3, c(1, 2, 5), pch = 4, col = "red", cex = 1.5, lwd = 2)
```

Pooling the branches of each regime gives much better estimates than rates per branch, and
the medians are close to the true ratios (red crosses), with a wide spread among trees.

**Turnover of partners.** With rates from `turnover_rates()`, the Spearman correlation between
the absolute rate RRphylo estimates on each tip branch and the turnover of partners of the
species, over 30 metacommunities on trees of 40 species:

```{r results-turnover}
round(summary(res$turnover$rho), 2)
```

The correlation is weak and varies among metacommunities: the turnover changes the rates of
tip branches only, and the same limit of one realisation per branch applies, so a signature
of assembly in the rates of single branches is hard to detect even when it is there by
construction.

## Limits

- Each branch carries one realisation of the process, which caps how well any estimator can
  recover the rate of a single branch; pooling branches, as in models with regimes, helps.
- The ecological dynamics of `turnover_rates()` and `food_web_rates()` inform only the tip
  branches, and the match between ecological time and branch length (`window`) is a choice,
  not a result of the simulation.
- The speeds of `food_web_rates()` are directional changes of the mean trait, so `k` sets
  relative rates, not an equivalence with Brownian variances.
